lead: In a mixture of three or more species, every pair has its own diffusivity, and the flux of one species depends on the gradients of all the others. One effective D is no longer enough. The Stefan–Maxwell equations keep one friction term per pair; Wilke's formula collapses them into a single effective diffusivity for a species moving through a stagnant mixture of the others. This decides the size of columns for multi-component distillation, the modelling of combustion, and the design of membrane and adsorbent pores where reformer gas is separated.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.3 for Fick's first law, and Chapter 1.4 for the equimolar and stagnant-film flux forms.

sections.h3: When two species are not enough

blocks.text: Two species need one number, D<sub>AB</sub>. Real streams carry more: reformer gas holds H₂, CO, CO₂, CH₄ and steam; flue gas carries N₂, O₂, CO₂ and H₂O; a distillation feed may have six hydrocarbons.

An n-component mixture has n species with mole fractions y₁, y₂, …, yn that add to 1. Every pair (i, j) has its own binary diffusivity Dij, measured or predicted as in Chapter 1.6. The number of pairs is n(n−1)/2: three for n = 3, ten for n = 5. Dij = Dji, so the table is symmetric with blanks on the diagonal.

Treat the mixture with a single effective diffusivity only when one species is dilute, or when the rest move as one block. When three or more species are present in comparable amounts, the motion of A is braked by B and separately by C, and those two brakes act through different pairs. The flux of A then depends on the gradients of B and C as well as its own. That is the multicomponent regime. It appears in multi-component distillation (see distillation), in combustion where radicals diffuse against burnt gas, and in narrow membrane pores.
Stefan and Maxwell wrote the balance as driving force against friction. For one-dimensional diffusion along z:
dy<sub>i</sub>/dz = Σ<sub>j≠i</sub> (y<sub>i</sub> N<sub>j</sub> − y<sub>j</sub> N<sub>i</sub>) / (c D<sub>ij</sub>)
blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> and y<sub>j</sub> are mole fractions; N<sub>i</sub> and N<sub>j</sub> are molar fluxes relative to a fixed frame, mol/(m²·s); c is the total molar concentration, mol/m³; D<sub>ij</sub> is the binary diffusivity of the pair i–j, m²/s; z is distance, m. The sum runs over every j other than i.

blocks.text: Read the right side as friction. Species i rubs against species j, and the rubbing grows with how fast they slip past each other. The slip shows up as (y<sub>i</sub> N<sub>j</sub> − y<sub>j</sub> N<sub>i</sub>), which is zero when i and j travel together. There are n such equations, but only n − 1 are independent, because the mole fractions add to 1.
Check the two-species case. For n = 2 the sum has one term: c D₁₂ dy₁/dz = y₁N₂ − (1 − y₁)N₁ = y₁(N₁ + N₂) − N₁. Rearranged:

blocks.where: the first term is the diffusion part and the second is the bulk-flow part carried by the mixture, in mol/(m²·s).

blocks.text: When the two fluxes are equal and opposite, N₁ + N₂ = 0 and plain Fick's law remains. When species 1 moves through stagnant 2, N₂ = 0, so N₁ = −c D₁₂ dy₁/dz / (1 − y₁), the stagnant-film form of Chapter 1.4. The Stefan–Maxwell set therefore contains both textbook cases inside it.

sections.h3: Wilke's approximation for a dilute species

blocks.text: Solving n coupled equations by hand is slow. Wilke's shortcut is derived for species i diffusing through a stagnant mixture of the others (every N<sub>j</sub> = 0 for j ≠ i). It is exact when the other species keep their ratios along the path and is a good estimate for any dilute species. The friction sum then collapses into one effective diffusivity:

blocks.where: D<sub>i,m</sub> is the effective diffusivity of species i in the mixture, m²/s; y<sub>i</sub> is the mole fraction of i; y<sub>j</sub> is the mole fraction of any other species j; D<sub>ij</sub> is the binary pair diffusivity, m²/s.

blocks.text: The value is then used inside Fick's law with the bulk term kept:

blocks.where: ΣN is the total molar flux of all species, mol/(m²·s). Drop the second term only when ΣN = 0, that is, equimolar counter-diffusion.

items: Notice the structure: the denominator adds y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>ij</sub>, so the resistances 1/D add, weighted by mole fraction. A pair with a small D<sub>ij</sub> (heavy friction) adds a large resistance.

D<sub>i,m</sub> is a local value. It depends on the composition at position z, and composition changes along the path. The flux equation must be integrated from z₁ to z₂, not multiplied by Δz. A shortcut using the inlet composition can be off by tens of percent over a long column.

In fine pores, wall collisions add a Knudsen diffusivity D<sub>K</sub>, and the two resistances combine as 1/D<sub>eff</sub> = 1/D<sub>i,m</sub> + 1/D<sub>K</sub>, the Bosanquet relation, which only a few universities teach.

figure.caption: The worked example. Wilke's formula for A uses only the two pairs that touch A: the resistances y<sub>B</sub>/D<sub>AB</sub> = 3.0×10⁴ and y<sub>C</sub>/D<sub>AC</sub> = 2.0×10⁴ s/m² add, giving D<sub>A,m</sub> = 0.90/5.0×10⁴ = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Averaging the D values instead would give 2.33×10⁻⁵ m²/s.

examples.question: A gas mixture at one atmosphere and 300 K has y<sub>A</sub> = 0.10, y<sub>B</sub> = 0.30 and y<sub>C</sub> = 0.60. The binary diffusivities are D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s, D<sub>AC</sub> = 3.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and D<sub>BC</sub> = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find the effective diffusivity of A in the mixture by Wilke's formula, and state how the answer would be used in Fick's law.
steps: Check the data. y<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>B</sub> + y<sub>C</sub> = 0.10 + 0.30 + 0.60 = 1.00, so the composition is complete.

Write Wilke's formula for the dilute species A: D<sub>A,m</sub> = (1 − y<sub>A</sub>) / (y<sub>B</sub>/D<sub>AB</sub> + y<sub>C</sub>/D<sub>AC</sub>). Only pairs that contain A appear, because the sum runs over j ≠ A. The B–C pair does not enter.
Compute the first resistance term: y<sub>B</sub>/D<sub>AB</sub> = 0.30 / (1.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s) = 3.0×10⁴ s/m².
Compute the second resistance term: y<sub>C</sub>/D<sub>AC</sub> = 0.60 / (3.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s) = 2.0×10⁴ s/m².

Use it as N<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>A,m</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz + y<sub>A</sub> ΣN. Compare with D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s: A moves through this mixture faster than through pure B alone, because C is the faster partner. If the composition changes along the path, D<sub>A,m</sub> changes too, and the flux must be integrated rather than multiplied by the path length.
examples.answer: The effective diffusivity of A in the mixture is D<sub>A,m</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
examples.check:
yA, yB, yC = 0.10, 0.30, 0.60
DAB, DAC = 1.0e-5, 3.0e-5
resistance = yB / DAB + yC / DAC
DAm = (1.0 - yA) / resistance
print(round(DAm, 10))

traps: Averaging diffusivities as y<sub>B</sub> D<sub>AB</sub> + y<sub>C</sub> D<sub>AC</sub>. Wilke's formula averages resistances, y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>ij</sub>, not D itself. The two answers differ in size and in trend.

Using N<sub>i</sub> = −c D<sub>i,m</sub> dy<sub>i</sub>/dz and forgetting the bulk term y<sub>i</sub> ΣN. That is valid only when ΣN = 0; for diffusion through a stagnant mixture it under-predicts the flux by the factor (1 − y<sub>i</sub>): 10 % at y<sub>i</sub> = 0.1, half at y<sub>i</sub> = 0.5.
Carrying one D<sub>i,m</sub> from the bottom of a column to the top. It is a local value tied to the local composition, so the flux equation has to be integrated.
Putting all n² diffusivities in a table. Only n(n−1)/2 are distinct, and D<sub>ij</sub> = D<sub>ji</sub>. Examiners like this count.

Mixing frames: the Stefan–Maxwell equations use N<sub>i</sub>, the flux relative to a fixed frame, not J<sub>i</sub>, the diffusion flux relative to the molar average velocity. The two differ by y<sub>i</sub> ΣN.

quiz.q: How many independent binary diffusivities does a four-component mixture need?
quiz.a: n(n−1)/2 = 4×3/2 = 6 distinct pairs, since D<sub>ij</sub> = D<sub>ji</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does Wilke's formula add y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>ij</sub> in the denominator instead of y<sub>j</sub> D<sub>ij</sub>?
quiz.a: Each term y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>ij</sub> is the friction that species j puts on i: friction grows with how much j is present and falls with how easily the pair slips (a large D<sub>ij</sub>). Frictions add, so the resistances 1/D<sub>ij</sub> add, weighted by y<sub>j</sub>, like resistances in series. An average y<sub>j</sub> D<sub>ij</sub> would let the easiest partner dominate; the resistance sum lets the hardest partner dominate, which is what the Stefan–Maxwell equations give. In the worked example the D-average would be (0.30 × 1.0 + 0.60 × 3.0)×10⁻⁵/0.90 = 2.33×10⁻⁵ m²/s, against the correct 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s.

quiz.q: A mixture has y<sub>A</sub> = 0.20, y<sub>B</sub> = 0.50, y<sub>C</sub> = 0.30, with D<sub>AB</sub> = 2.0×10⁻⁵, D<sub>AC</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁵ and D<sub>BC</sub> = 1.5×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find D<sub>A,m</sub>.
Using D<sub>A,m</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s held constant, c = 40 mol/m³, find the steady flux of A through stagnant B and C over a 2.0 mm film when y<sub>A</sub> falls from 0.10 to 0.05.
quiz.a: Stagnant means ΣN = N<sub>A</sub>, so N<sub>A</sub> = (c D<sub>A,m</sub>/L) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)]. cD/L = 40 × 1.8×10⁻⁵ / 0.002 = 0.36 mol/(m²·s). Ratio = 0.95/0.90 = 1.0556, ln = 0.0541. N<sub>A</sub> = 0.36 × 0.0541 = 0.0195 mol/(m²·s).

quiz.q: In a mixture where D<sub>AB</sub> is much smaller than D<sub>AC</sub>, explain what Wilke's formula predicts for D<sub>A,m</sub> as y<sub>B</sub> falls from 0.6 to 0.1, and why.
quiz.a: The term y<sub>B</sub>/D<sub>AB</sub> dominates the denominator while y<sub>B</sub> is large, because 1/D<sub>AB</sub> is large. As y<sub>B</sub> falls, that resistance shrinks and the smaller resistance 1/D<sub>AC</sub> takes over, so D<sub>A,m</sub> rises towards D<sub>AC</sub>. The effective diffusivity is not a mole-fraction average: it is controlled by whichever species offers the largest resistance at that composition.

beyond: Not for the exam. Process simulators solve the full Maxwell–Stefan set instead of Wilke's shortcut, and pore models for adsorbents combine molecular and Knudsen diffusion in the dusty-gas model. Search for Maxwell–Stefan equations and the dusty-gas model.
